title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 208: Quenching the Deluge: China's Sponge City Revolution
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 208 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

Quenching the Deluge: China's Sponge City Revolution

Paragraph 1. Many big cities in China have grown very fast over the past forty years. Builders covered wet lands, farms, and small rivers with hard stone and concrete. When heavy rain falls on hard concrete roads, the water cannot sink naturally into the ground. Old pipes under the streets were made for light rain, not big storms. In July 2021, huge rains flooded the city of Zhengzhou, filling subway stations with water and causing heavy damage.

Paragraph 2. To stop future floods, China started a new project called the 'Sponge City' plan. Professor Yu Kongjian led this clever idea. Earlier builders tried to push rainwater out of cities quickly using rigid concrete pipes. Instead, Professor Yu says cities should act like soft sponges that drink up rain, clean it, and release it slowly. On city streets, workers replace concrete ditches with green channels planted with native grasses and bushes. Beneath the soil, gravel and sand filter out dirt before clean water sinks deep underground.

Paragraph 3. Parks and city squares also use new building materials. Workers replace solid stone tiles with special bricks that have tiny holes. These porous bricks are made from recycled factory waste called slag, allowing rain to pass straight into the earth. In the city of Wuhan, engineers also built huge rainwater parks along rivers. During dry weather, people walk on wooden paths, play sports, and enjoy green gardens in these parks. During heavy storms, the parks hold millions of litres of floodwater, which later drains into city lakes or dries into the air.

Paragraph 4. Turning old city centres into sponge cities is still expensive and hard. The ground under busy streets is already full of subway tunnels, water pipes, and power cables. Also, green parks can quickly fill up when extreme storms drop a whole month of rain in three hours. Still, many countries around the world are studying China's sponge cities to stay safe from wild weather.
